message.reasoning_content:
Let me understand the situation. This is the "improvement" phase. I must call design.decide_improvement exactly once (delivery tool). The task: Independently select whether to change one or both weights and their values: adopt with a nonempty effective delta, or defer/reject with empty changes.

Key facts available: baseline terminal_tip_speed_weight = 0.0, holding_tip_speed_weight = 0.0 (from summary recipe). Terminal reach passed (0.0076 m < 0.01 m). Holding window failed: position error 0.0076–0.0581 m, speed 0.635–1.581 m/s vs limits 0.01 m, 0.02 m/s. sampled_settling_passed = false, holding_speed_passed = false. So the dominant failure is holding speed — speeds 30-80x the 0.02 m/s limit. Both weights are currently 0.0.

The editable scope: control/recipe/terminal_tip_speed_weight and control/recipe/holding_tip_speed_weight, both [0,1], new positive values >= 0.0001, effective delta required.

The diagnosis: accepted diagnosis says holding_window_residual_tip_motion is "possible" — position error sometimes fine, speed always failing. The clear actionable lever: holding_tip_speed_weight (per-second squared spatial speed weight on nodes at/after settling-window start) directly penalizes residual tip speed in the holding window. That's the most relevant weight given speed is failing at 30-80x limit.

terminal_tip_speed_weight is dimensionless terminal weight on squared world tip speed / tip_speed_scale_m_s; it's currently 0. Reach already passes (terminal error 0.0076 m inside 0.01). But the terminal speed is 0.6351726092425104 m/s = same as holding speed minimum. Interesting — terminal speed 0.635 m/s which is ~32x the 0.02 m/s scale. Terminal tip speed weight could reduce the final approach speed and thus improve holding speed at the entry to the window. But the main failing window is the whole 0.05 s.

Also there is a diagnostic indication that computation (~17.26 s mean update, 35/35 deadline misses, ~15 s optimization solves, stopping_counts Solve_Succeeded=1 / User_Requested_Stop=34) — that's a real concern: does adding speed weights cost more computation? Yes, plausible adverse effect. But the question is whether to adopt. The instruction says missing proof of causality alone does not prohibit this bounded experiment; availability status etc. There's one backend solve remaining (project_remaining backend_solves: 1). Also local_comparison capability: two solves, <=300 charged seconds, at a saved baseline update with effective horizon 0.01 s. Hmm, but numeric budget: local_solves: 2 remaining. But wait — local comparison requires a legal saved state with effective horizon 0.01 s. The baseline updates have effective_horizon 10, 7, 5 control intervals (0.1, 0.07, 0.05 s) — none is 0.01 s? Effective horizon must be 0.01 s = 1 control interval at 0.01 s period. Hmm, cataloged effective_horizon values: 10, 7, 5 control intervals — none equal 1. So no legal saved update with effective horizon 0.01 s is displayed. That means local_comparison probably not legal. Let me check: "Optional only when the supplied campaign grant permits it: compare baseline against one selected changed positive weight at a legal saved state." The grant: "at a saved baseline update with effective horizon 0.01 s". We only have effective_horizon values 10, 7, 5 in the catalog. Not all 35 are cataloged though. Hmm. The fact_catalog only shows some. But the instructions warn: "Not currently displayed does not mean never queried." However, we also must not invent. We cannot certify a legal saved update with effective horizon 0.01 s exists. Given uncertainty, safest is to omit local_comparison. Actually, hmm, but omission is allowed ("omit if unnecessary"). I think omit — because we can't confirm a legal saved state (effective horizon 0.01 s) from evidence, and we shouldn't force it.

Wait, but is a local comparison useful? The improvement phase's key deliverable is the decision. Given budget tightness (backend_solves remaining = 1) hmm, actually numeric budget says remaining prediction_evaluations 0, local_solves 2. And project_remaining backend_solves = 1. So the complete experiment (one model-selected changed candidate complete simulation) would use the single backend solve presumably at a later phase. Our decision just records intent.

Now the decision: adopt with a nonempty effective delta. Which weight(s)? The failing criterion in the holding window is speed (all six samples exceed 0.02 m/s), and position error also fails at larger rows (max 0.0581 m). The holding_tip_speed_weight is directly designed for that: penalize squared tip speed at nodes at/after settling-window start. Given speeds are 32-79x the limit, this is the relevant lever. Terminal reach already passes, so changing terminal_tip_speed_weight risks... actually terminal tip speed weight would penalize terminal speed, which is currently 0.635 m/s, also way above 0.02 — it might help decelerate. But the terminal weight is dimensionless with tip_speed_scale 0.02 m/s, so (0.635/0.02)^2 = ~1008 times weight — a huge gradient. Selecting a value: careful. If we set terminal_tip_speed_weight = 0.001, the terminal cost contribution would be 0.001 * 1008 = ~1.0, comparable to terminal_weight 5.0 times position error? Actually terminal_weight 5.0 times squared position error: (0.0076/... hmm position_error_scale_m is null) — anyway.

Hmm. But maybe I should keep it simple and change just one weight: holding_tip_speed_weight, since holding speed is the failing criterion, and holding window is where the failure occurs. Changing both adds risk and confounding. The instruction: "Independently select whether to change one or both weights and their values". The grant capability: "At most one model-selected changed candidate" for the complete experiment; local comparison: "select one changed positive weight".

I think the strongest, most defensible bounded experiment: adopt holding_tip_speed_weight = some positive value, and defer/reject terminal? Hmm — but the tool has one changes object; disposition is one of adopt/defer/reject. The changes can include one or both parameters. If I adopt with only holding weight nonzero, that's a single-parameter change. Should I also set terminal? The failure is in holding; terminal reach passes; adding terminal speed weight could disturb a passing reach criterion (adverse). But terminal speed is 0.635 m/s at the terminal instant which coincides with minimum holding speed — actually the terminal instant presumably is the last sampled time 0.35, and terminal speed 0.6351726092425104 equals the holding speed minimum. So the terminal speed and holding speed are related. Still, the holding weight covers the whole window including the final node, so it subsumes.

Hmm — wait, does holding weight apply at nodes at/after the settling-window start; the terminal node is at/after window start, so the holding weight already penalizes the terminal speed. So adding terminal weight is redundant-ish. So a single changed parameter: holding_tip_speed_weight.

Value selection: must be >= 0.0001, <= 1.0. What magnitude? The speed cost is per-second squared spatial speed weight. Given speed is ~30-80x limit, the speed term squared = (1.581)^2 per second... The existing velocity_weight is 0.0001 and terminal_weight 5.0. Hmm. Without deeper analysis, choosing a modest, non-saturating value like 0.01 or 0.001. Hmm. I need to be careful not to "select a developer-prescribed value" — there's no prescribed value given. I should pick a defensible value and state the rationale.

Let me think about scale: holding cost = weight * sum over holding nodes (dt-weighted) of ||v_tip||^2 (spatial speed squared, per second). With tip speeds ~0.6–1.6 m/s across 5 nodes with dt 0.01 → sum of v^2 ≈ 5 * ~1.0 ≈ 5 (m/s)^2... times dt? "integration-step-weighted" so ≈ 0.01*5 = 0.05 (m)^2/s-ish. Meanwhile tracking cost: tracking_weight 1.0 * position error^2 (scaled by position_error_scale, null → maybe just error^2) ≈ 0.01^2 = 1e-4 to (0.058)^2=3.4e-3. Hmm. So with weight 0.01, the holding speed cost contribution ≈ 0.01*0.05 = 5e-4, comparable to tracking position cost. With weight 1.0, it'd be 0.05, dominating tracking. Hmm, but I shouldn't invent derived numerical facts. The instructions: "Derived numbers require a retrieved computation result; do not invent a derived numerical fact." So I must avoid stating computed numbers as facts. Rounded prose is allowed, but I shouldn't present an invented derived numeric claim.

I'll pick holding_tip_speed_weight = 0.01? Or 0.05? Hmm. Let me think about what will actually help without destabilizing. Actually maybe a moderate value like 0.01 is reasonable — it's 100x the existing velocity_weight 0.0001, and 1/100 of terminal_weight 5.0. Hmm, but units differ (per-second vs dimensionless) so comparisons are apples-to-oranges.

I'll go with 0.01 for holding_tip_speed_weight. Hmm, alternatively 0.001. Let me pick a value that's clearly meaningful but not saturating. Honestly, given speed exceeds the limit by ~30-80x, a weight strong enough to matter matters. I'll state 0.01 with rationale that it's a modest fraction of the terminal_weight scale and 100x the velocity_weight, chosen to be clearly nonzero but far from the bound 1.0, leaving headroom for a later increase if the effect is directionally right but too small.

Hmm, but should I also consider that the real dominant problem is computation (17 s per update on a 0.01 s period, 35/35 deadline misses) — 1 second max_cpu_s? No, max_cpu_s 30.0, feasible_return budget 15 s. The solve hits the 15 s budget → "User_Requested_Stop" 34 times, meaning 34 of 35 solves were terminated at the 15 s feasible-return budget, i.e., plans are not converged to tolerance. So the controller is running on stopped-at-budget plans. Adding weights may increase per-iteration cost marginally but the budget-cap behavior suggests solve time won't change much (it's budget-limited, not convergence-limited). That's a good point for the expected computation effect: solve time is dominated by the 15 s feasible-return budget (User_Requested_Stop in 34/35 updates), so a changed weight is unlikely to reduce or increase wall time substantially — but this is a hypothesis not proof. Also note budget_s 15.0 matches observed ~15 s solves.

Also adverse effects: adding holding speed weight may slow the terminal approach, potentially increasing terminal position error (risking the currently-passing reach criterion) — but terminal reach is already inside tolerance and the holding speed term acts in the settling window; the risk is position error grows or the tip stops short of the goal. Also increased objective terms could change solver behavior; and since 34/35 plans terminate at budget without convergence, the weight change may have little effect if the solve is not converged (or conversely more).

Observations that would weaken the hypothesis: holding speed unchanged or worse; position error exceeding limit further; terminal error leaving the 0.01 m tolerance; solve wall time increasing beyond the budget or unusable updates appearing.

Also I should note the accepted diagnosis statuses: holding_window_residual_tip_motion = possible; one_step_projection_error_explains_holding_speed = insufficient_evidence; computation explanation supported but not causal to holding. So hypothesis: residual tip speed in the holding window; the holding speed weight directly targets that.

Should I include terminal_tip_speed_weight? Let me decide: change only holding. Rationale: reach already passes, terminal weight targets the terminal instant only, and the terminal instant is inside the holding window already covered by the holding weight; changing two parameters at once would confound the attribution of the single available complete experiment. Good, defensible, and the grant allows selecting one or both.

Hmm, however: is there an argument that holding_tip_speed_weight requires "explicit settling settings"? "Requires explicit settling settings." The config has settling {position_limit_m 0.01, speed_limit_m_s 0.02, window_s 0.05} — yes, explicit settling settings present in summary detail.summary.controller.parameters.data.settling. So the requirement is satisfied. Good — I should state that as a fact-based check. Wait — but I don't have a fact handle for the settling block. The fact catalog has detail.summary.settling_criteria.speed_limit_m_s etc. and window? There's detail.summary.settling_criteria.position_limit_m? Not in catalog; there is detail.summary.settling_criteria.speed_limit_m_s (febbe3c381492) and detail.summary.settling_criteria.speed_limit_m_s again (ff4e96a9aa48c). Also recipe holding_tip_speed_weight 0.0? Not in catalog either. Hmm, the catalog is a compact subset. But the summary_content in handoff includes the recipe with holding_tip_speed_weight: 0.0 and settling settings. That's explicit handoff content (in the request/working memory). Good enough — the values are handed over with the request content. But fact handles? I should reference handles where I have them. The tool call parameters don't include fact handles though — the design_decide_improvement schema only has disposition, rationale, expected_measurable_effect, changes, local_comparison. So no fact_selectors needed. Good, simpler. The instructions mention "Select fact_handles for your own concise factual statements" — but the tool schema has no such field. "Never invent missing business fields." So I just supply the allowed fields.

So the call:

disposition: "adopt"
changes: {"control/recipe/holding_tip_speed_weight": 0.01}
rationale: explain hypothesis, why relevant, baseline value 0.0, etc.
expected_measurable_effect: separate on reach, holding position, holding speed, computation.
local_comparison: omit? Or include with update_id? It requires "Saved baseline controller update; effective plan horizon must be 0.01 s." We only know effective horizons 10, 7, 5 — none 0.01 s. So we cannot nominate a legal saved update. Omit and note in rationale that no saved update with effective horizon 0.01 s was identified in the displayed evidence, so no local comparison is requested.

Hmm, but should I make a read to check for a legal update with effective horizon 1? The fact catalog: detail.evidence.observations.updates[1].effective_horizon value 10 (update 9), updates[2].effective_horizon 10 (update 10), updates[1].effective_horizon 7 (update 28), updates[0].effective_horizon 10 (update 24), updates[3].effective_horizon 5 (update 30), updates[7].effective_horizon 10 (update 7). None is 1. Also "historical_unrecorded_horizons" unsupported. So a legal saved state with effective horizon 0.01 s (=1 control interval) is not displayed; and the horizon appears fixed at 10 configured with reductions to 7/5 near the end. So local comparison is not available. Omit.

Alternatively I could do one evidence read to check... but phase_tools are ["evidence.read","design.decide_improvement"], and evidence_turn_limit 0, turns used 0. Hmm, "evidence_turn_limit": 0 in phase_progress but the instruction says "Use exactly one call, or up to three independent evidence reads." Hmm, that's the generic instruction. The phase budget: model_calls limit 3, remaining 3. Given the evidence_turn_limit is 0, extra reads may be pointless. Actually the top-level instruction says use exactly one call, or up to three independent evidence reads. But the phase says "When the read allowance ends, deliver the current phase using its remaining advertised handoff tool." evidence_turn_limit 0 suggests no read turns. I'll just do the single design call. Hmm — but the decision would benefit from confirming effective_horizon values? Not necessary; can't nominate anyway.

Hmm, actually, would a local comparison be valuable and permitted with some update? Only if a legal saved state with effective horizon 0.01 s exists. Given evidence suggests horizons are 5–10 intervals (0.05–0.10 s), no. Omit — the schema says "omit if unnecessary."

Now write the rationale and expected effects carefully, distinguishing evidence-supported statements from hypotheses, with coverage caveats.

Draft rationale:
"Accepted diagnosis support: the failing sampled criterion includes holding-window tip speed — all six samples of the 0.30–0.35 s window exceed the 0.02 m/s limit (0.635–1.581 m/s) while position error is inside 0.01 m at the smallest sample and outside at the largest (0.058 m); terminal reach passes at 0.0076 m. Both editable weights are 0.0 in the saved recipe, so each currently contributes no speed cost. Hypothesis: adding a nonzero holding-window tip-speed cost will penalize residual spatial tip speed at nodes at and after the settling-window start, which is exactly the criterion that fails, so the optimizer should prefer plans whose settling-window trajectory is slower at the tip. I select the holding weight rather than the terminal weight because terminal reach already passes, the terminal instant is itself inside the penalized window, and changing both at once would confound the single complete-experiment comparison the grant allows. Explicit settling settings are present (window 0.05 s, position limit 0.01 m, speed limit 0.02 m/s), satisfying the holding weight's requirement. Value 0.01: clearly effective (>=0.0001) yet 1/100 of the configured bound and modest relative to the existing terminal_weight 5.0, leaving headroom. Coverage limits: only six holding rows and batched endpoint samples were displayed; trajectory-wide speed was not characterized; the diagnosis rates the residual-tip-motion explanation only 'possible', so this is a bounded test, not a causal claim. Local comparison omitted: no saved baseline update with effective horizon 0.01 s is displayed (cataloged effective horizons are 5, 7 and 10 control intervals at a 0.01 s period), so a legal paired state is not available to nominate."

Hmm — careful about "1/100 of the configured bound" — that's fine (0.01 vs 1.0 is arithmetic, not invented derived data... it's a simple stated ratio; acceptable, but maybe keep simple: "well below the 1.0 bound"). Avoid invented derived numbers. I'll say "well below the 1.0 upper bound and above the 0.0001 minimum" — that's fine.

Also mention computation: the 15 s feasible-return budget and 34/35 User_Requested_Stop means solve wall time may be budget-limited rather than convergence-limited, so weight change may not change solve duration much — but this is a hypothesis to check, not a derived fact. I'll phrase as "recorded stopping_counts Solve_Succeeded=1, User_Requested_Stop=34 (from the handed-over summary)" — hmm, is stopping_counts in the fact catalog? Not in catalog handles, but is in summary_content (handed-over common summary, explicitly handed over — read_ledger shows common_summary explicitly handed over with 4 displayed handles). Yes, it's in the handed-over content. Fine to cite as "run summary reports". OK.

expected_measurable_effect: "Reach: terminal tip position error should stay at or below the 0.01 m tolerance; a move toward the goal at higher speed would be an adverse result and would be reported as reach degradation. Holding position: sampled holding-window tip position error across the six 0.30–0.35 s rows should not grow and ideally shrink below the 0.01 m limit at all six rows (baseline maximum 0.058 m). Holding speed: sampled holding-window tip speed should fall toward or below the 0.02 m/s limit at all six rows (baseline range 0.635–1.581 m/s); a smaller-but-still-above-limit reduction would count as directionally consistent. Computation: mean_update_s, deadline_misses and per-update optimization_solve_s should be compared against the baseline 17.26 s mean and 35/35 misses; because 34 of 35 solves were stopped by the feasible-return budget (Solve_Succeeded 1, User_Requested_Stop 34), I expect solve wall time to remain budget-limited rather than to scale with the new cost, but an increase in update wall time, deadline misses, or unusable updates would be an adverse effect."

Should I mention "expected effects separately on reach, holding position, holding speed and computation" — yes, done.

Also "observations that would weaken the hypothesis" — include in rationale or expected_measurable_effect. Better in rationale or maybe a sentence in expected effect. I'll add to rationale: "Evidence that would weaken this hypothesis: unchanged or higher holding-window tip speeds, new or larger position errors in the window, terminal error leaving the 0.01 m tolerance, or a substantial rise in solve wall time."

Length is fine. One tool call.

Also "Recommendation disposition and next action are independent" — fine.

Let me also double check: minimum for new positive selections 0.0001; 0.01 ok. Effective delta required — baseline 0.0 → 0.01 is effective. Good. Only one changed parameter.

Write the call.

function.arguments: {"disposition": "adopt", "changes": {"control/recipe/holding_tip_speed_weight": 0.01}, "rationale": "Accepted diagnosis (possible, bounded): the failing sampled criterion includes holding-window tip speed — across all six recorded rows of the 0.30–0.35 s window every sampled tip speed exceeds the 0.02 m/s limit (0.635–1.581 m/s), while the smallest sampled position error (0.00764 m) is inside the 0.01 m limit and the largest (0.05814 m) is not; terminal reach passes at 0.0076 m against the 0.01 m tolerance. The saved recipe shows holding_tip_speed_weight = 0.0, so the holding window currently carries no tip-speed cost at all. Hypothesis: the settling failure includes residual tip speed inside the settling window, and adding a nonzero per-second squared spatial tip-speed cost at nodes at/after the window start makes the optimizer prefer settling-window trajectories that are slower at the tip, which is directly the criterion that fails. Weight relevance: holding_tip_speed_weight is defined on exactly those nodes, and explicit settling settings are present (settling window 0.05 s with position limit 0.01 m and speed limit 0.02 m/s), satisfying the parameter's requirement. I select the holding weight alone rather than also changing terminal_tip_speed_weight: terminal reach already passes, the terminal instant lies inside the penalized holding window anyway, and changing both at once would confound the one model-selected complete experiment the grant allows. Value 0.01: clearly effective (above the 0.0001 minimum for a new positive selection) and well below the 1.0 bound, deliberately modest relative to the configured terminal_weight so that a directional effect can be seen without saturating the trade-off, leaving room for a later bounded increase if the effect is right but too small. Coverage and limits: this rests on six holding rows plus batched endpoint samples and run-level scalars, not a trajectory-wide characterization; trajectory-wide holding co-variation was not displayed; the diagnosis rates the residual-tip-motion explanation only 'possible' and the one-step-projection explanation 'insufficient_evidence'; no closed-loop counterfactual replay or causal attribution capability exists, so this is a bounded test of a stated hypothesis, not an adoption of a proven cause. Observations that would weaken the hypothesis: unchanged or higher holding-window tip speeds; new or larger holding position errors; terminal error leaving the 0.01 m tolerance; sampled holding speed falling only for one row while others stay far above the limit; or a material rise in update wall time, deadline misses or unusable updates. Local comparison deliberately omitted: the grant requires a legal saved baseline update with effective horizon 0.01 s, and no such update is identified in the displayed evidence (cataloged per-update effective horizons are 5, 7 and 10 control intervals at a 0.01 s control period), so no legal paired state can be nominated.", "expected_measurable_effect": "Reach: terminal tip position error should remain at or below the recorded 0.01 m tolerance (baseline 0.0076 m); any increase past tolerance is an adverse result and would be reported as reach degradation. Holding position: the six sampled 0.30–0.35 s tip position errors should not grow and ideally all fall inside the 0.01 m limit (baseline range 0.00764–0.05814 m). Holding speed: the six sampled holding-window tip speeds should fall toward or below the 0.02 m/s limit (baseline 0.635–1.581 m/s); a consistent reduction that still stays above the limit counts only as directionally consistent, not as a passed criterion. Computation: mean update duration, deadline_misses and per-update optimization solve time should be compared with the baseline records (mean update about 17.26 s against a 0.01 s control period, 35 of 35 deadline misses, and solver-status counts of 1 success versus 34 user-requested stops at the 15 s feasible-return budget); because nearly all solves terminated on that budget rather than on convergence, I expect wall time to stay budget-limited rather than scale with the added cost, but an increase in update wall time, deadline misses, unusable updates, or constraint violation would be a measurable adverse effect. Full historical warm plans and optimizer iteration traces are not retained, so per-iteration cost attribution cannot be checked.", "local_comparison": null}
